reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO
clinicalPearls: A tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by an orthonairovirus, transmitted mainly by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with blood or tissues of infected livestock
In India it is a recognised emerging threat, with documented outbreaks in Gujarat and neighbouring regions and cases among livestock handlers and healthcare workers
Onset is abrupt with fever, severe headache, myalgia, and prostration, progressing over days to a haemorrhagic phase with petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding, and multi-organ involvement
Nosocomial and slaughterhouse transmission is well described, so a history of tick exposure, animal contact, or care of a bleeding patient is a critical clue
Laboratory features include thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and rising transaminases, with deranged coagulation heralding severe disease
This is a medical emergency requiring strict infection-control and barrier precautions, patient isolation, and safe handling of body fluids and laboratory specimens
Management is chiefly supportive with careful correction of coagulopathy and organ support; suspected and confirmed cases must be promptly notified to public health authorities
reference.pathophysiology: CCHF virus is an enveloped RNA virus that, following tick bite or exposure to infected blood or tissues, replicates and disseminates widely. It infects endothelial cells and cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system, and a dysregulated inflammatory and cytokine response together with direct endothelial injury leads to increased vascular permeability, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and haemorrhage. Hepatic involvement and marrow suppression contribute to the coagulopathy and cytopenias, and severe cases progress to shock and multi-organ failure.
additionalDifferentials: Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, Lassa, hantavirus, Kyasanur Forest disease)
Meningococcaemia and other bacterial sepsis with DIC
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR for CCHF viral RNA in early illness, performed in an appropriately biosafe laboratory
CCHF-specific IgM and IgG serology later in the course
Full blood count, coagulation profile, liver and renal function to gauge severity
Careful exclusion of dengue, malaria, and leptospirosis given overlapping presentations
All sampling and testing conducted under enhanced biosafety with prior laboratory notification
redFlags: Spontaneous mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding, extensive ecchymoses, or evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation
Rapidly falling platelet count with rising transaminases and deteriorating coagulation
Hypotension, shock, or signs of multi-organ failure
Any suspected case demands immediate isolation, barrier nursing, and public health notification because of nosocomial transmission risk
reference.prognosis: Case fatality is high, especially with delayed recognition and severe coagulopathy or multi-organ failure; early supportive care and meticulous infection control improve outcomes, and survivors who pass the acute haemorrhagic phase generally recover.
pitfalls: Failing to institute isolation and barrier precautions early, exposing staff and other patients to a highly transmissible pathogen
Anchoring on dengue or malaria and overlooking CCHF in someone with relevant tick or livestock exposure
Performing invasive procedures or unprotected phlebotomy that increase bleeding and transmission risk
Not notifying public health authorities and the receiving laboratory before sending specimens
management: Institute strict barrier and infection-control precautions with patient isolation, safe handling of body fluids and laboratory specimens, and prior laboratory notification
Consider early antiviral therapy with the nucleoside analogue ribavirin, recognising that the evidence base is uncertain
Provide meticulous supportive care with intravenous fluid resuscitation and organ support in a critical care setting
Correct coagulopathy and cytopenias with blood products such as packed red cells, platelets and fresh frozen plasma as required
Avoid intramuscular injections, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and other agents that aggravate bleeding
Monitor full blood count, coagulation profile and liver and renal function to gauge and track severity
Notify public health authorities, trace contacts and healthcare workers with symptom surveillance, and consider ribavirin post-exposure prophylaxis
